title: Which wealth is the true wealth?
claim: Several verses award the title of true or only wealth to different things: grace, hearing, not wanting, and learning, and 751 says nothing but wealth counts. Commentators read each against material wealth, so these may be a rhetorical form rather than one ranking.
audit_issue: Five of the six named holders rest on sound links; energy rests only on the weak 592-400, though the verse does say it. Overstated: 'keeps awarding' describes six verses of 1330. The commentators read each superlative against material wealth, so the verses rarely compete with each other on their own reading; only 751 versus 400 is a head-on clash. One sound link is a reversed duplicate. The note on 751-400 wrongly speaks of 'each book's register': both verses are in the Book of Wealth.

title: Superlatives that compete
claim: The formula recurs beyond wealth and sometimes collides: nothing surpasses virtue, yet nothing surpasses apt speech; nothing beats truth, yet not killing is ranked above it; poverty is unmatched pain, yet wealth under a tyrant hurts more. Commentators reconcile the first two, and 323 is a deliberate ranking, so these superlatives need case-by-case reading.
audit_issue: Fails on restraint (32-122 is only a shared formula; restraint is a kind of virtue) and 92-225 is forced. The last sentence overreaches: 323 is an explicit ranking and Parimelazhagar treats it as settling the order, so not every superlative is mere praise.

title: Absolute ethics and the needs of the state
claim: Five rules stated without exception in the Book of Virtue meet specific verses in the Book of Wealth that suspend or limit them: killing, anger, hypocrisy, generosity and purity of mind. The verses do not acknowledge this; Parimelazhagar reconciles some by adding limits such as royal duty and enemies only. The Book of Wealth elsewhere upholds ethics (546, 657).
audit_issue: All five named areas have a sound link, though two links are the same pair. Overstated in three ways: 480 limits generosity rather than reversing it; 'often' for commentators' added limits rests on clear cases at 550 and 829; and Parimelazhagar directs 303 at renunciants, so some rules were not universal for him. Counterevidence against a book-wide pattern: 546 and 657 show the Book of Wealth upholding ethics.

title: Echoes of the earlier books in the Book of Love
claim: A few lover-speakers reuse the earlier books' language against its grain: shame worth dying for is set aside to save life (1132/1017), the body-soul bond called flimsy in 338 becomes the image of union (1122), and honour's ban on following those who slight you is called unavailable to the lovesick (1255/966). These are dramatised speeches and do not overturn the earlier teaching.
audit_issue: Of the four named examples only shame holds. Senses and warrior are contrasts without incompatibility, and backbiting is forced because அலர் is not புறங்கூறல். 'Overturns' is false as a claim about the book: these are dramatised speakers in stated situations, on Parimelazhagar's and Manakkudavar's framing, and do not revise the earlier teaching.

title: Where the man and woman differ
claim: On Parimelazhagar's speaker assignments, the man and woman differ over shame (1132/1163) and memory (1202/1207), and 1137 states the first contrast outright. Manakkudavar assigns some speakers differently, and most other differences in the Book of Love follow union and separation rather than gender.
audit_issue: Only shame and memory hold, and memory's gender contrast fails on Manakkudavar, who gives 1202 to the woman. Evening, night and leaving fail: most contrasts are union against separation, not man against woman, and two links lie outside the Book of Love. Counterevidence: 1251 has the woman's shame break, and the man suffers in 1132 and 1268. 1137, the verse that states the asymmetry outright, is not among the links.

title: Truth defined by what it does
claim: On Parimelazhagar's reading, chapter 30 defines truthfulness by harmlessness of effect and explicitly sets aside mere statement of what happened, though 293 still treats lying as going against what one knows. That definition carries real weight: without it, 297's unbroken not-lying and 292's blameless falsehood would conflict.
audit_issue: The second sentence holds (292-297). 'Not agreement with fact' is Parimelazhagar's explicit gloss on 291, not the verse's wording, and 291 appears only in a forced link, so most links do not test the claim. Counterevidence: 293 still treats lying as going against what one's own heart knows, in the same chapter.

title: Is the world's moral order just?
claim: The Kural says the upright do not fall (170, 210), yet treats the prosperity of the crooked and ruin of the upright as a puzzle (169), and it both accepts the apportioner (377) and curses the world's maker if begging was decreed (1062). The verses leave this open; Parimelazhagar resolves it through past deeds.
audit_issue: Promise, admission and protest hold (170, 210, 169, 1062, 377). Fails on verse 1, which makes no moral claim, and on 'explains misery as deserved' as an opposite of the protest (330-1062 weak). 'Without resolving them' holds for the verses only: Parimelazhagar resolves 169 and 170 through past deeds, and his 1062 keeps past deeds too. 169 may be hypothetical on his 'if they occur'.

title: Fate and agency, across the whole book
claim: Chapter 38 makes effort and sloth products of fate, while other verses treat effort and heedlessness as within a person's power and say persistence puts fate behind you. Commentators narrow the conflict, but the verses pull apart. The phrase தான் முந்துறும் at 380 and 1023 is an echo, not a conflict.
audit_issue: Well supported by 371-620, 620-380, 609-371, 429-380 and 482-376. The closing point about தான் முந்துறும் is a true verbal echo but rests on a weak link and shows no conflict. 'Treat them as chosen' is strictest for 609 and 620. Parimelazhagar narrows the conflict at 620 and Manakkudavar at 429, which the claim doesn't mention.

title: Poverty: a discipline and a catastrophe
claim: The Kural disagrees with itself on whether worth survives poverty (988 against 1044) and on whether the world despises the poor (752 against 841). இன்மை also names the ascetic's chosen possessionlessness, but that is a different condition from destitution.
audit_issue: 'Whether character survives poverty' holds (988-1044, 532-408). The first sentence is a word overlap for two different conditions, and 'householder' is not in the verses. 'Whether anything is worse' has no sound link here (657-1041 is not a clash), though 558 and 841 against 1041 in another thread do support it. Parimelazhagar's gloss at 532 largely eases the understanding clash.

title: Birth: denied in one verse, assumed in many
claim: Besides denials of birth's rank (972; also 409 for learning), the book also treats birth as a real factor: integrity is natural to the well-born (951), friends are screened by family (793, 794) and birth is named as a source of courtesy (992). Quoting 972 alone gives a partial picture.
audit_issue: Friends and integrity hold; officials (502) rest only on a weak link. 'Denied in one verse' is false: 409, in the thread's own links, also subordinates birth, and 133 redefines it by conduct. 'Usually quoted' cannot be checked from this corpus. On Parimelazhagar's reading 972 keeps varna work-differences, so it denies less than the thread implies.

title: Where does understanding come from?
claim: The book names at least three sources of understanding that do not sit easily together: study (396), one's own or fated nature (373) and company (454). Parimelazhagar reconciles study with fate by limiting study's reach to where fate does not oppose it. Separately, it is divided on whether a speaker's standing matters (423, 415, 850).
audit_issue: Only study against fate or innate nature and against company hold. Hearing rests on the wrong 396-416, and poverty's absence has no link in this thread. The two sound links on 423 concern a speaker's credibility, not sources of understanding. Parimelazhagar explicitly reconciles 396 with 373, which the thread does not mention.

title: Can signs be trusted?
claim: The face is said to show the heart (706), yet enemies' smiles are said to hide hostility even from the face (824) while their words are soon seen through (826). Tears publish love in 71 and may conceal a weapon in 828, but those verses concern different people and do not conflict.
audit_issue: The face and enemies' faces hold (706-824, 824-826). Spies and tears rest on weak links, and 'lovers feign indifference' has no link at all. 'Tears prove love' overstates 71: enemies' false tears do not contradict it.

title: Giving and asking
claim: Giving is valued for itself and for its returns. Asking is permitted from the right person and also called the worst thing a tongue can do. Consecutive chapters open in direct opposition.
audit_issue: Holds on 1051-1061, 1054-1066, 222-1051 and 211-226. 'For itself' rests on 222 and 211. Fair to say the consecutive chapters open opposed. Caution: the note's 'edge of death' attribution at 1051-1061 was not found in the commentary available, and 780-1066 should go.

title: What can friendship survive?
claim: The book says those devoted to friendship do not leave a friend (791) yet leaving a fool's friendship is gain (797), and says friendship grows with practice (783) yet does not need it (785). Parimelazhagar supplies the limit: exit is for what one took on unknowingly (800). Old friends who harm you are kept (807), which he treats as a separate case.
audit_issue: 'A friend can't be left' against leaving a fool, and practice against no practice, hold, though the second is mild. 'Old friends may ruin you' is true of 807 but its clash with 800 is weak. The final sentence is speculative and partly wrong, since Parimelazhagar does state a limit at 800 (what one took on unknowingly) and 805 gives a character-versus-lapse distinction.
